keyVerseText: And out of the ground made the LORD God to grow every tree that is pleasant to the sight, and good for food; the tree of life also in the midst of the garden, and the tree of knowledge of good and evil.
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun מַרְאֶה (marʼeh) derives from the root רָאָה (râʼâh), which fundamentally means 'to see' or 'to look.' This root conveys not merely physical sight but also perception, discernment, and experience. Thus, מַרְאֶה carries the sense of that which is seen—an appearance or vision—emphasizing the act and result of looking. This etymological background enriches the word beyond a simple 'appearance' to include the relational dynamic of perceiving and responding to what is observed.
usageInScripture: With 103 occurrences, מַרְאֶה is used broadly to denote sight, appearance, and vision, both natural and supernatural. The top translations such as 'as the appearance,' 'favoured,' and 'to look upon' reveal a semantic range from physical form or countenance to the experience of beholding something desirable or significant. This consistency shows מַרְאֶה as a versatile term that captures both the external form and the inner perception of what is seen, whether a person, a phenomenon, or a divine vision.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding מַרְאֶה is crucial for grasping biblical themes of revelation and divine-human encounter. It highlights that God’s self-disclosure engages the human faculty of sight—not just physical but spiritual perception—inviting believers to behold His glory and character. This word also reminds us that appearances in Scripture often carry deeper realities, pointing to God's beauty, favor, and the patterns He sets for life. From an evangelical perspective, marʼeh underscores the truth that faith involves seeing beyond the surface to the divine presence and providence behind what is visible.
keyVerseReflection: Genesis 2:9 states that God caused every tree to grow that is 'pleasant to the sight' (מַרְאֶה) and good for food, emphasizing the visual delight and desirability of creation. Here, מַרְאֶה conveys more than mere appearance; it reflects God's intentional design for beauty and goodness that draws the human eye and invites appreciation. This verse affirms that God's creative work is not only functional but also aesthetically pleasing, pointing to His character as the ultimate source of both beauty and provision.
